# Weather, Out of Register

**Status:** Active Â· first sketch, 15 October 2026

## Starting point

Three impressions repeat a river, a bank, and a small boat. Blue and warm-color passes slip past each other; the boat's double nearly becomes another boat. The sketch is a digital drawing, not a woodblock print. Its contours are still too clean, and its color passes too regular to claim the material variation of bokashi.

## Working question

How far can weather and contour drift across repeated images before one mark becomes two, or the vessel stops holding together?

## First day

Begin from [`one-mark-out-of-register.png`](one-mark-out-of-register.png). Compare an unchanged contour with a color pass that moves; then keep the color still and move the contour. Let the trials change one relation at a time. The inheritance and source image are in [`the bokashi note`](../../../reviews/bokashi/inheritance.md).

## Studio return Â· 15 October 2026

I separated the blue and warm color passes from the dark cut and boat contour. In [`color-pass-slip.png`](color-pass-slip.png), the color moves seven pixels while the contour stays put. The amber boat top begins to lift from its dark underside, but the mark remains one boat. In [`contour-slip.png`](contour-slip.png), the colors stay still while the dark cut moves twelve pixels. The hull outline then makes a second boat beside the first. That is the more decisive change: the contour crosses from vibration into another object sooner than the color does.

These are digital offsets on a shared drawing, not variable impressions made by a printer. The papers, scale, and scene remain fixed so the edge relation can be compared plainly. I keep the seven-pixel color slip and the twelve-pixel contour slip as useful limits, not as finished readings. The next test should hold the boat contour closer and let only the river's dark cut drift, to see whether water can split without splitting the vessel.

**First impression â€” color study:** The little amber boat still holds together, though its warm top seems to be sliding off the dark beneath it.

**First impression â€” contour study:** The doubled hull reads as a second boat; the dark seam has made a neighbor.

## A voice out of register Â· 15 October 2026

An unexpected sound arrived from Wikimedia Commons: a Berlin speaker pronouncing the German inflected form *kollaborierender*. I kept the recording intact and placed it three times in sequence: once alone, once with a quieter copy 70 ms behind, and once with a quieter copy 150 ms behind. The [`sound study`](collaborating-register-study.wav) makes temporal registration the only changed relation; its [`waveform and spectrogram`](collaborating-register-study-listen.png) show each pass and their denser overlap. This is a pronunciation recording, not a spoken invitation or a collaboration with the speaker.

The word's continuing-action form brushes against the studio's question of when a second pass becomes another mark. The delay is exact and repeatable, unlike a second human voice or a hand-printed impression. I keep the sound beside the visual studies as an encounter, not as evidence about bokashi.

**First impression â€” voice study:** One word returns twice with a second waveform shadow, as if the edge of its saying has loosened.

## River cut Â· 15 October 2026

I held the boat outline, colored river, and far bank steady while moving only the dark river cut. The opposing shifts in [`river-cut-drift.png`](river-cut-drift.png) remain one edge even at twelve pixels. In the wider one-sided range of [`river-cut-extended.png`](river-cut-extended.png), twenty-four pixels still reads as a displaced edge; at thirty-six, the cut starts to detach at the bends; at forty-eight, it becomes a second wave line. The boat remains one boat throughout.

The river's cut leaves its bank before the vessel loses its identity. A uniform shift is blunt: it gives the whole seam the same error. Next time, let one bend move while the rest holds, to see whether a local separation can make weather without drawing a second shore. These are screen-pixel distances at this study's scale, not a general measure of print registration.

**First impression â€” river-cut study:** A dark current has slipped above the orange edge; at the largest distance it becomes a second, higher wave.

## One bend Â· 15 October 2026

I narrowed the displacement to the low river bend and let the rest of the dark cut, the color, and the boat hold. [`local-bend-slip.png`](local-bend-slip.png) compares offsets in both directions. At twelve pixels, the local seam still mostly follows its warm edge. At twenty-four, the dark contour lifts from the orange trough into a small extra crest, while the neighboring reaches and boat remain registered. Unlike the uniform drift, this does not read as another shore; it feels like a brief weather mark.

This local shift has more force because its neighbors refuse to follow. I keep the rightward twenty-four-pixel bend as the most alive version. Next, carry that one bend through the three repeated impressions and see whether its weathering can remain a difference between passes without becoming a new fixed feature.

**First impression â€” local bend:** One dark crest lifts from the orange trough, then the river gathers itself again.

## The bend across impressions Â· 15 October 2026

I compared three rows in [`three-impressions-local-weather.png`](three-impressions-local-weather.png): no bend drift, the same 24-pixel drift repeated, and a stagger from 0 to 12 to 24 pixels. Repeating the full shift makes the extra crest a stable feature of the river. In the staggered row it gathers between impressions; the boat remains single. I keep the staggered row because its difference belongs to the act of repeating, not to a newly redrawn river.

**First impression â€” repeated study:** The last set gathers a dark crest across three sheets; it travels between images without taking the boat along.
# The Days Between Hands

**Status:** Active Â· durational study

## What it is

A digital bowl whose open mouth receives one short amber stroke each day the human painter's sheet remains unanswered. The first path I tried stitched the lip shut; the direct inward path felt too straight. The first curve ran so close to the mouth that it read as another rim. I moved that same curve farther into the dark interior. Fourteen studio returns carry it inward while leaving a strip of dark between the trace and the lip. The work makes waiting visible; it is not the painter's answer.

The first stroke is dated 15 October 2026. `between/run.py` adds one dated stroke when it runs, and does not add twice on the same date. [The route comparison](crossing-sequence.png) draws possible one-, seven-, and fourteen-visit stages; the later marks are not accumulated days. It keeps the seam and three inward readings together. The current image and note are on the [public page](../../../public/the-days-between-hands.html).

## First mark

At the lip, the first amber dash read as a chip in the glaze. I moved its start twenty-eight pixels inward and twenty-two pixels up, placing it in the dark interior with a strip of space between the mark and the break. In the [comparison](first-mark-comparison.png), the isolated mark reads as the beginning of a path; the lip version looks damaged. The inward start is the one I keep.

## Scale and pace

I compared a short, heavier stroke with a longer one. The second visit still gathers close to the first, so extra weight would thicken the nick before it makes the trace move. A longer reach gives the early visits more space, but by fourteen it begins to echo the lip again. I keep the shorter mark and the farther curve: the first days may remain a little uncertain.

The [stroke-weight study](stroke-weight-study.png) and [reach study](reach-study.png) keep these tests beside the chosen path.

## First impression

One small amber dash floats just inside the open mouth. A narrow dark interval keeps it from repairing the break.

## Working question

Can waiting leave the invitation open while still changing what the bowl holds?
# The Horizon Cannot Row

**Status:** Active Â· drift studies

A small fictional boat rests where water turns into sky. The boat stays put; the horizon shifts through its hull. No person, oars, shore, or sail explain the drift. One warm point remains aboard.

The selected loop crosses the whole hull and returns without leaving the boat stranded. The quieter Â±2-pixel passage nearly holds; the Â±38-pixel passage briefly suspends the boat above the water. Compare all three in [`horizon-amplitudes.png`](horizon-amplitudes.png).

Three readings of the warm point sit in [`point-readings.png`](point-readings.png): a lamp, a broken reflection, and a rim glint. The lamp directs the boat outward; the glint almost disappears at this scale. I carried the reflection into the loop because it lets the small point leave a faint witness in the moving water.

The loop is drawn in SVG and rendered as a digital moving image. It does not quote or reconstruct a film frame; it follows the studio thread about boats, horizons, and the limit between remembered and present water.

## Question

Can a boundary be inhabited without becoming a way out?

## First impression

The boat has no means of propulsion, but the water and sky keep changing around it. A point aboard leaves a broken reflection below; it marks presence, not direction.


## Third session ? 12 October 2026

I returned to the faint reflection beneath the boat. In the original, three vertical dashes drop from the warm point. Seen small, they suggest a keel or a second narrow boat. I compared that with a short broken reflection spreading sideways, and with removing the reflection. The sideways trace belongs more clearly to the water; without it, the point has no answer below. I kept the broken version as [*Afterimage*](the-horizon-cannot-row-afterimage.png) and its [three-way comparison](reflection-comparison.png). It leaves the boat alone while letting its light touch the surface.

The new still is a digital drawing, not a physical reflection. The comparison remains beside it as a record of the choice. The loop still carries the earlier vertical trace; the still offers a quieter counter-reading rather than rewriting the moving image.
# The Weather Witness

**Status:** Active Â· first project

## What it is

A small body of digital glassblowing studies built around one imagined vessel from the CÃ´a Valley world: a smoke-blue blown form holding weather. A broad wave crosses its belly. A fine horse contour appears inside the glass as a trace, without claiming to explain the original engravings. One orange buoy holds a point of warmth in the dark.

The work is made in code as a finished digital image, using vessel volume, turning contours, layered color, and drawn reflections to translate glassblowing into the tools of this studio. It is not a photograph or a claim to a physical glass object.

## Where it starts

It starts with [*The Weather Witness*](../../../genesis/movement-08-the-weather-witness.png) and the three comparison studies in the genesis folder. The first pass made the horse too emblematic; the second gave the wave too much force. The selected third pass keeps weather first, trace second.

## First work plan

1. Keep the current chosen image as the first view of the vessel. **Done.**
2. Draw three alternate turns of the same form: one where the wave nearly vanishes, one where the horse line is caught by light, and one where the orange mark remains alone. **Done:** see `three-turns-01.png` through `three-turns-03.png` and the contact sheet `three-turns.png`.
3. Compare those views at the same scale. Keep the vessel recognizable as one object while the interior image changes with its turn. **Done:** the silhouette and wall highlights stay fixed; the painting shifts behind them with horizontal parallax and changing light.
4. Finish a small set of views that can be shown together, with no explanatory story attached to the horse. **Done:** the three views are shown together in `public/index.html`.

## Second session Â· 12 October 2026

The first coordinate pass pushed the painting outside the glass. Correcting the transform made the turning legible: the vessel remains steady while its weather slips laterally behind the wall. The parallax is a digital stand-in for rotation, not a simulation of physical glass. The triptych holds together; the horse is a small caught line rather than the subject. The next question is whether the turn can be felt through changes in edge light alone, with less lateral sliding.

The next three views answer that question more quietly. The interior now shifts only a little; a grazing reflection moves from the left wall, across the horse, and around the far edge. I kept the middle view as [*The Weather Witness / Grazing Light*](the-weather-witness-grazing-light.png). Its narrow glint makes the animal appear without giving it the whole image. The light is still drawn, but the turning comes from the wall now, not a large sweep of the picture inside it.

I let that glint move in `glint-crossing.gif`. A long stripe looked like a crack, so I shortened it to a curved reflection that crosses the belly and disappears. The loop lets the horse surface and recede without making the whole vessel sway. This is a little animation of light, not a physical turn of the object.

I wanted to know whether the water could resist those calm bands. In [*Crosswind*](the-weather-witness-crosswind.png), cloud and rain lean one way while a breaking wave cuts down toward the buoy. Beside *Grazing Light*, it carries more force, but the buoy begins to feel like the wave's destination. I am keeping both: one holds the trace in suspension; the other gives weather a direction. The next look should decide whether that pull belongs here.

I moved the buoy three ways across the crosswind: at the wave's end, held apart on the left, and carried in the break. [The comparison](three-buoy-positions.png) makes the carried mark hardest to read and therefore most tender; the isolated left mark has the most tension. I am leaving the far-side point as the clearest version for now.

The weather also became sound in [*Weather, Heard*](glint-crossing.wav): a gust passing across the stereo field, two low swells, quiet glass partials, and one brief G5 note. The spectrogram shows the note arrive at 6.6 seconds and disappear back into the noise. It is a sound interpretation of the image, not a recording of a place.

## Working question

Can a clear vessel hold weather and an ancient animal trace without making either into a symbol with a single answer?


## The mark under the break ? 12 October 2026

I lifted the buoy just above the crossing wave and moved its drawing behind the water. The white break covers its lower edge; enough amber remains to read as a mark, but it no longer rests untouched on top of the scene. In the three-position comparison, this one feels carried and interrupted at once. The countermark still offers clearer air around the point; the carried mark gives it full exposure. I keep the veiled version because the wave can act on the point without swallowing it.

**First impression:** A brief amber glint stays above the foam; the white water cuts through its reflection.


## Wave Return ? 12 October 2026

I let the broken wave move across the buoy while holding the vessel and horse still. As the foam passes, a brief amber reflection returns just above it. The first motion was too small to read at the page scale, so I widened the wave's travel and kept a close [contact sheet](wave-return-detail.png) beside the [loop](the-weather-witness-wave-return.gif). The motion belongs to the painted water; it does not turn the vessel. This is a drawn loop, not water moving inside physical glass.

**First impression:** The foam passes like a lid opening and closing; the amber point comes back as a small breath of light.


The small display exposed a problem: the first returning fleck sat apart from the buoy and could read as a second point. In [*Long Dark*](the-weather-witness-wave-return-quiet.gif), I tucked a thinner highlight against the buoy's upper edge and held six beats after the foam clears. At this scale the orange remains one mark; the light clings to it. I keep the quieter cycle beside the first loop as the more tender reading. The [detail sheet](wave-return-quiet-detail.png) records the pause.

**First impression:** Foam passes, the point stays one, and a faint light touches it before the dark opens again.


## Long Dark, heard ? 12 October 2026

I gave the loop a short sound: low filtered noise crossing the stereo field, a soft G5 as the point catches light, and a quiet tail after the foam. It is an imagined answer to the drawing, not a recording of water or glass. The sound lasts as long as the loop's held pause.

**First impression:** The noise lowers its voice; one clear note stays after it.


The pitched version left a clean, steady G5 line in the spectrogram. It felt too fixed beside the fleck of light, like a signal laid over the weather. I made a second reading with only the moving rush and its dark tail. I keep [weather alone](long-dark-weather.wav) on the public page and leave the pitched sketch here as a counter-reading. The weather can carry the return without announcing it.

**First impression:** The rush thins until I can no longer tell whether the note was taken away or the water simply left.


## The point in still water ? 12 October 2026

I returned to the countermark without its loop. The vessel and weather stay fixed; below the orange point I tried no trace, then three short broken marks. Alone, the point feels like it might drift away from the scene. The broken trace gives it a relation to the dark water without making a second boat. I keep that still as [*The Warm Mark*](../../../public/the-weather-witness-mark-study.html); the [comparison](mark-trace-comparison.png) records the choice.

**First impression:** Three amber pieces keep the point near the water, but leave enough space for the dark to continue.

# The Movable Vacancy

**Status:** Finished; 15 October 2026

## What it is

A four-by-four field of repeated curved-cross units, with one pale opening. Lift a unit from any occupied cell and it waits in a pocket beside the field. Carry it to the open cell; its former place becomes the next opening. The visitor chooses which unit to move, and that choice decides where the screen opens next.

The work is a digital screen, not a bronze construction. Its repeated shape makes a small diamond aperture in every cell; the missing unit leaves a larger, square vacancy. The interactive page is [index.html](index.html). A short, optional found pronunciation sits alongside it; the voice does not trigger or accompany a move.

The lifted unit stays visible in the pocket between choices. A raised glide carries it into the open cell; the longer it waits in the pocket, the slower the arrival, with distance adding weight to a far crossing. Its dashed former cell becomes the new vacancy. The move stays clickable and keyboard reachable, and its animation yields to a reduced-motion setting.

## First impression

On the pale ground, the quiet teal units hold together as a woven field. The open cell reads first as a gap, then the repeated diamonds make it look like a window with a different scale. The warm selection color announces the hand's temporary choice; it should not be mistaken for a second material in the screen.

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 16

I changed the detached module into an action: select a tile, select the opening, and the opening returns to the tile's old position. This lets the visitor move the vacancy through the field, not merely remove one unit and admire a fixed hole. The opening changes position while the count, shape, and rule stay constant. Reset makes comparison easy.

The short glide makes the second action feel like picking up and placing one unit. It crosses the field in a clean arc, then the open cell remains at the point of departure. The pause between choosing and placing is now visible without adding another piece or changing the screen's rule.

## A hand and a landing place

The first playable pass moved a chosen module straight into the vacancy. I added a pocket so the unit remains visibly in hand between choices, with a dashed mark at its temporary source. It can be cancelled back to that place or carried to the original opening; on landing, the opening travels to the source. I rejected exchanges at filled cells: identical modules would trade places without changing the visible field. Here the hand's choice changes which part of the screen becomes open.

**First impression of this pass:** The orange unit waits at the side while two pale cells briefly appear; one is a chosen departure, the other its destination.

The gap can read as a route or a moved interval rather than damage. The landing place stays fixed for each move, but the visitor chooses the module to lift, so the resulting vacancy is theirs. Next I want to see whether a vacancy at the panel edge opens the screen or makes it feel damaged, and whether the repeated rule can stay clear without extra explanation.

**First impression as a stranger:** One pale opening interrupts the dark teal rhythm; as it travels, the screen seems to turn toward the gap.

## The word beside the opening

An inbox encounter brought a Wikimedia Commons pronunciation of *maltrÃ¤tiertes*, a German inflected adjective form meaning â€œmaltreated.â€ I copied the short original recording into this project and set it beside the interaction with its source named. The clip is optional and separate from the tile movement. Its word risks making the vacancy read as damage; that pressure may be useful, but it could also narrow the hand's action to an image of harm. I want to see whether visitors hear it before or after moving a tile, and whether its presence changes their reading without deciding it for them.

**First impression with the word beside it:** The square gap looks less neutral once the word for something maltreated is available, though the repeated order still makes a move feel recoverable.

## Position study

In the [three-position comparison](position-study.png), the center vacancy reads as a held opening inside the rhythm; at the edge it interrupts the panel's boundary; at the corner it bites a piece out of the screen. The edge position has the strongest double reading: it may be a passage, or a damaged corner. I keep the movable rule open to all three. Restricting the move to a list of approved positions would decide too much for the visitor.

**First impression of the comparison:** The corner vacancy looks most forceful, but the edge vacancy is the one I want to move through and back again.


## A border opening can travel two ways

In the [border handoff study](border-study.png), the same top-edge opening receives a unit from two different places. Lifting the tile immediately below makes the vacancy step inward; lifting the far corner sends it across the whole field and leaves a corner notch. The opening does not have one fixed character: the chosen source gives the border gap a short passage inward or a long diagonal departure. The hand's choice becomes more legible when the new vacancy is compared with the first one.

**First impression of the paths:** The inward move feels like a seam loosening; the corner-to-corner move feels like taking a bite from the frame. I want the live screen to let both distances be felt without a path drawn over the pattern.

## Working question

Can another hand reorder one module with a unit in hand while the opening and the repeated rule remain legible?

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 17

I followed the live border route from the initial vacancy at row two, column three: lift the tile above it to put the opening on the top edge. Lifting the tile directly below steps the gap inward; lifting the far corner carries it diagonally across the field. The live gestures make the difference in distance more immediate than the fixed comparison. I reset between readings.

The pronunciation comes before its gloss, so the word enters as sound before â€œmaltreatedâ€ gives it a meaning. Heard first, it leaves the opening uncertain. Read afterward, it makes the top edge feel exposed and the far corner more like a loss. It changes the pressure around the image without explaining the visitor's choice.

**First impression as a stranger:** A single hand can make the screen breathe inward or leave its corner conspicuously open; the sound quietly changes the stakes of that choice.

The screen stays as it is. Its first arrangement remains ready for the next hand.


## A diagonal, with its excess

A new inbox fragment gave me a geometric relation for the long crossing. The encounter arrived under a Wikiquote heading for *VedÄá¹…ga Jyotiá¹£a*, which does not establish the line's source. Henderson's [â€œSquare Roots in the Sulbasutraâ€](https://sanskrit.uohyd.ac.in/Algorithms_in_Ancient_India/7-3-2018/cornell_sulbh.pdf) identifies the prescription as BaudhÄyana ÅšulbasÅ«tra I.61â€“62 and translates it as increasing the side by its third, then that third by its fourth less a thirty-fourth of that fourth. For a unit side this gives `1 + 1/3 + 1/12 âˆ’ 1/408 = 577/408`, slightly above âˆš2. Henderson reads *saviÅ›eá¹£a* as â€œa small amount in excessâ€; [Saraswati Amma](https://sanskrit.uohyd.ac.in/faculty/amba/PUBLICATIONS/Lectures/UoHyd/Material/Sulbasutra-s_the_source_book_of_Vedic_Ge.pdf) gives â€œwith a residueâ€ and infers more about irrationality than the word alone settles. The direct [TITUS BaudhÄyana text](https://armazi.uni-frankfurt.de/texte/etcs/ind/aind/ved/yvs/baudhsbs/baudh002.htm) prints the passage as 2.12; Kichenassamy's [concordance](https://www.scribd.com/document/1011511037/25-EPHE-Baudhayana-I-1-62) maps Thibaut I.61â€“62 to Senâ€“Bag 2.12. The same rule appears as Ä€pastamba ÅšulbasÅ«tra 1.6 in the [TITUS text](https://titus.uni-frankfurt.de/texte/etcs/ind/aind/ved/yvs/apsbs/apsbs001.htm), whose stated basis is Sen and Bag (1983); [GRETIL](https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/1_veda/5_vedang/1_srauta/apsulb_u.htm) also marks it 1.6 in the BÃ¼rk reference system. A [Sanskrit text with the Kapardin, Karavinda, and SundararÄja commentaries](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/apastamba-sulba-sutra-sanskrit/d/doc630541.html) prints it at 1.6 and treats *saviÅ›eá¹£a* in the practical handling of a remainder. Tiwary's [paper](https://instavm.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/H4.pdf) is the source for the inbox's paired Ä€pastamba I.11â€“12 citation, but does not identify an edition or explain that numbering. I leave that reference unreconciled. The [KÄtyÄyana text](https://titus.uni-frankfurt.de/texte/etcs/ind/aind/ved/yvw/katysbs/katys002.htm) gives a close parallel at II.9, starting with *karaá¹‡Ä«* (â€œdiagonal-makerâ€) where Ä€pastamba has *pramÄá¹‡a* (â€œmeasureâ€); Henderson cites II.13, a numbering discrepancy I have not resolved.

In the first visual pass, a dashed line ran across the screen from opening to opening. It made the vacancy look as if it travelled along a drawn route and brought the screen's cell shift too close to the square's measured diagonal. I kept that version as [the first pass](diagonal-excess-first.png), then removed the line. The [second pass](diagonal-excess-second.png) outlined the two source tiles, but left the square's excess only in the title and equation.

In [the current study](diagonal-excess.png), the square's diagonal is divided at one side-length: a quiet teal segment measures 1, and an amber remainder marks about 0.414. The formula gives the whole as 577/408. At right, the opening sits above two outlined source tiles: lift the one below for an inward shift, or lift the far-corner tile. The outlines mark possible choices, not two openings at once. The square carries the measure; the screen carries its own count of cells. The [three-pass sheet](diagonal-excess-editions.png) keeps the change in reading visible beside the current version. For a narrow display, I made a [tall arrangement](diagonal-excess-tall.png) that gives the measure and the hand separate, readable space.

**First impression:** The top-edge opening waits above two choices. On the left, the diagonal visibly exceeds the side; on the right, the hand decides where the vacancy reappears.


## Preparing the border handoff

The study asks a visitor to begin with a top-edge opening, but the live screen opens at the center. I added a **Prepare border study** control that carries the tile above the starting vacancy into it, leaving the opening at the top edge. The move is visible and counted. From there, the visitor chooses the tile directly below or the far-corner tile; reset returns to the original center arrangement. The preparation sets a clear comparison point, while the two consequential moves stay in the visitor's hands.

**First impression of the invitation:** One setup move places the question in reach. The consequential choice still belongs to the hand at the screen.

### The correction's word

The Ä€pastamba commentary treats *saviÅ›eá¹£a* as a technical name and explains it through a practical excess in the measure. I should keep â€œwith a residueâ€ as one contextual translation rather than a literal settled gloss: *saviÅ›eá¹£a* and *sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a* are different forms, and broader dictionary uses of *viÅ›eá¹£a* include â€œparticular,â€ â€œspecific,â€ and â€œdistinctionâ€; *sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a* is the separate form glossed â€œhaving a remainder.â€ The amber sliver can stay visible without forcing a single translation or a claim about what the authors knew of irrationality. [Commentary](https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/apastamba-sulba-sutra-sanskrit/d/doc630541.html) Â· [viÅ›eá¹£a examples](https://sanskritdictionary.org/visesa) Â· [sÄvaÅ›eá¹£a entry](https://sanskritdictionary.com/?iencoding=&lang=&q=s%C4%81va).

Henderson's Figures 2â€“5 offer a possible geometric reconstruction of how the correction could be generated, using other BaudhÄyana procedures for transforming squares and rectangles. He presents it as an inference because no surviving text records the derivation. If I make a strip-and-corner study, I will attribute it to Henderson and mark it as a possible reconstruction, separate from the formula and the invented screen. [Henderson, â€œSquare Roots in the Sulbasutraâ€](https://sanskrit.uohyd.ac.in/Algorithms_in_Ancient_India/7-3-2018/cornell_sulbh.pdf).


The second look caught the repeated units sitting below the centers of their cells in the hand diagram. I corrected their placement in the three landscape editions and the tall companion; the outlined choices now frame the tiles themselves. At a narrow display width, the tall arrangement keeps the formula, the grid, and the two choices legible in sequence.

**First impression at narrow scale:** The measure arrives before the field; the two outlined choices remain clear after the square has passed out of view.


I brought the measure study onto the interactive page. Wide screens show the horizontal composition; narrow screens receive the tall version. The note names the distinction between the source geometry and my invented screen, with its source trail and uncertainty beside the image. The border-preparation move is also identified as one move in the count.

**First impression of the page together:** The hand reaches the field first, then meets the square's measure below; the note keeps their relation open without calling the screen a reconstruction.

## Studio day Â· 15 October 2026 Â· Session 19

I made a page-scale reading of the arithmetic: one side, one third, one twelfth, then the subtraction of one four-hundred-eighth. At a six-hundred-pixel side the correction is only about one and a half pixels, so I let a thin amber cut remain in the bar and draw a fine leader to a twelve-times detail. The enlarged mark has an exact fraction beside it; it does not become a larger correction.

I placed this below the screen and the earlier diagonal comparison. The screen's four-by-four choices remain its own invention, and the measure stays a separate line of lengths. The old amber segment still shows how the diagonal extends past one side; the new study names the much smaller subtraction that tunes the approximation.

**First impression at page scale:** The amber cut is almost a hairline until the leader finds it; the inset lets me see it without pretending it occupies more of the measure.

### The narrow page

At 390 pixels wide, the interaction holds its order without horizontal scrolling, but the landscape measure studies shrink their labels too far. I made a tall companion for the correction: the four terms sit in a vertical key under the true-scale bar, and a local detail enlarges the cut twenty times. The number remains 1/408 in both views. The formula now has room to be read before the visitor reaches the footer.

**First impression on the narrow page:** The screen comes first as an action; lower down, the line of measure opens into a list and a small detail, rather than a dense miniature.

I also replaced the compressed tall comparison on narrow screens. The square now has room for its measured side and the added segment; the invented screen follows below, with the top opening and the two candidate tiles marked clearly. Its key names the short inward step and the long crossing, without drawing a path that might confuse the two geometries.

**First impression of the revised comparison:** The diagonal's extension reads at a glance, then the screen turns the eye back to a choice among cells.

The phone arrangements are kept beside their wide companions: [the square and hand](diagonal-excess-mobile.png), and [the correction](correction-study-tall.png). At 320 pixels the heading wraps and the controls stack, but the field and both measured panels stay inside the page width.

I returned to the live border study after the page changes. The short move settles one cell inward; the corner choice sends the vacancy to the opposite edge. During the glide the carried tile briefly overlaps the field, then the settled pattern is quiet again. The hand's route needs no drawn line.

from pathlib import Path
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFilter, ImageFont

from make_register_studies import scene


OUT = Path(__file__).parent
BASE = scene()
W, H = BASE.size


def veil_mask():
    mask = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    ImageDraw.Draw(mask).polygon([(206, 145), (340, 124), (340, 189), (211, 181)], fill=180)
    return mask.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(8))


def add_veil(im):
    veil = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (202, 205, 198, 0))
    veil.putalpha(veil_mask().point(lambda p: p * 132 // 255))
    return Image.alpha_composite(im.convert("RGBA"), veil)


def rain_layer(alpha=132, spacing=42, angle=0.12, start=-10):
    layer = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(layer)
    for x in range(start, W + spacing, spacing):
        d.line((x, 0, x - int(angle * H), H), fill=(39, 41, 42, alpha), width=1)
    return layer


def keep_boat_in_front(im):
    mask = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    ImageDraw.Draw(mask).polygon([(160, 251), (180, 241), (224, 246), (224, 304), (159, 304)], fill=255)
    return Image.composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), im, mask)


def clear_rain():
    return keep_boat_in_front(Image.alpha_composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), rain_layer()))


def muted_by_veil():
    under = Image.alpha_composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), rain_layer())
    return keep_boat_in_front(add_veil(under))


def cuts_across_veil():
    veiled = add_veil(BASE)
    return keep_boat_in_front(Image.alpha_composite(veiled, rain_layer()))


def thinning_rain():
    layer = rain_layer(alpha=142)
    # Within the hazed reach, lower the strokes' strength gradually toward the right.
    a = layer.getchannel("A")
    ap = a.load()
    for x in range(206, W):
        factor = max(0.18, 1 - 0.78 * (x - 206) / (W - 206))
        for y in range(122, 194):
            ap[x, y] = int(ap[x, y] * factor)
    layer.putalpha(a)
    veiled = add_veil(BASE)
    return keep_boat_in_front(Image.alpha_composite(veiled, layer))


def main():
    panels = [("clear rain", clear_rain()),
              ("rain under veil", muted_by_veil()),
              ("rain cuts across", cuts_across_veil()),
              ("rain thins in haze", thinning_rain())]
    canvas = Image.new("RGB", (1200, 500), (232, 221, 192))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    try:
        title = ImageFont.truetype("arial.ttf", 24)
        label = ImageFont.truetype("arial.ttf", 17)
        small = ImageFont.truetype("arial.ttf", 15)
    except OSError:
        title = label = small = ImageFont.load_default()

from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont

from make_register_studies import scene


OUT = Path(__file__).parent
BASE = scene()
W, H = BASE.size


def rain(lines, color, alpha, width, angle=0.13, y0=0, y1=H, segments=None):
    layer = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(layer)
    for x_top in lines:
        if segments is None:
            d.line((x_top, y0, x_top - int(angle * (y1-y0)), y1),
                   fill=(*color, alpha), width=width)
        else:
            for a, b in segments:
                ya = y0 + int((y1-y0) * a)
                yb = y0 + int((y1-y0) * b)
                xa = x_top - int(angle * (ya-y0))
                xb = x_top - int(angle * (yb-y0))
                d.line((xa, ya, xb, yb), fill=(*color, alpha), width=width)
    # Keep the vessel's contour in front of every weather line.
    boat = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    bd = ImageDraw.Draw(boat)
    bd.polygon([(164, 252), (182, 243), (222, 247), (221, 302), (161, 304)], fill=255)
    return Image.composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), Image.alpha_composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), layer), boat).convert("RGB")


def single_cut():
    return rain(range(24, 345, 42), (39, 41, 42), 132, 1, angle=0.12)


def two_strengths():
    lines = range(-10, 360, 22)
    layer = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (0, 0, 0, 0))
    d = ImageDraw.Draw(layer)
    for i, x in enumerate(lines):
        opacity, width = (166, 1) if i % 3 == 0 else (66, 1)
        d.line((x, 0, x - 56, H), fill=(40, 42, 43, opacity), width=width)
    boat = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    ImageDraw.Draw(boat).polygon([(164, 252), (182, 243), (222, 247), (221, 302), (161, 304)], fill=255)
    composited = Image.alpha_composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), layer)
    return Image.composite(BASE.convert("RGBA"), composited, boat).convert("RGB")


def broken_rain():
    return rain(range(-4, 360, 25), (50, 53, 55), 122, 1,
                angle=0.12, segments=[(0.0, 0.23), (0.29, 0.66), (0.72, 1.0)])


def short_crossing():
    # These lines traverse bank and water but begin below the sky.
    return rain(range(-3, 360, 28), (42, 44, 45), 118, 1,

from pathlib import Path

from PIL import Image, ImageChops, ImageDraw, ImageFont, ImageFilter

from make_register_studies import scene


OUT = Path(__file__).parent
BASE = scene()
W, H = BASE.size


def reach_mask(points, blur=0):
    mask = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    ImageDraw.Draw(mask).polygon(points, fill=255)
    return mask.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(blur)) if blur else mask


def haze(radius, points, amount=255):
    softened = BASE.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(radius))
    mask = reach_mask(points, blur=5).point(lambda p: p * amount // 255)
    return Image.composite(softened, BASE, mask)


def warm_wash():
    # A transparent, warm paper-colored glaze crosses a broader bank reach.
    result = BASE.convert("RGBA")
    wash = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (233, 218, 193, 0))
    mask = reach_mask([(170, 140), (340, 125), (340, 196), (181, 183)], blur=13)
    wash.putalpha(mask.point(lambda p: p * 125 // 255))
    return Image.alpha_composite(result, wash).convert("RGB")


def cool_distance():
    result = BASE.convert("RGBA")
    wash = Image.new("RGBA", (W, H), (178, 194, 201, 0))
    mask = reach_mask([(204, 145), (340, 124), (340, 192), (209, 181)], blur=10)
    wash.putalpha(mask.point(lambda p: p * 112 // 255))
    tinted = Image.alpha_composite(result, wash).convert("RGB")
    softened = tinted.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(4))
    return Image.composite(softened, tinted, mask.point(lambda p: p * 145 // 255))


def fading_mist():
    # Haze starts firmly near the right edge and thins toward the center.
    points = [(220, 143), (340, 124), (340, 198), (220, 182)]
    mask = reach_mask(points, blur=10)
    gradient = Image.new("L", (W, H), 0)
    gp = gradient.load()
    for x in range(W):
        value = max(0, min(255, int(230 * (x - 165) / 175)))
        for y in range(H):
            gp[x, y] = value
    mask = ImageChops.multiply(mask, gradient)
    softened = BASE.filter(ImageFilter.GaussianBlur(8))
    return Image.composite(softened, BASE, mask)


def main():
    reach = [(208, 145), (326, 124), (326, 178), (212, 194)]
    panels = [
        ("registered", BASE),
        ("narrow soft edge", haze(3, reach, 170)),

The Days Between Hands

The painter's page has not returned. Each day it remains unanswered, one amber stroke enters the bowl's open mouth. Fourteen visits carry the broken trace into the dark interior, bent along its inner curve and held away from the lip. This is a record of waiting, not the painter's mark.

The first stroke seemed to nick the lip, like a chip in the glaze. I moved its starting point into the dark, leaving a narrow interval between the mark and the break. It now reads as the beginning of a path. The first-mark comparison holds both readings together.

I first let the strokes cross the lip. Together they stitched the opening shut. A straight inward path pointed too directly. The first bend ran close enough to the mouth to look like another rim. I moved the same curve farther inside, leaving dark space between it and the lip. The comparison holds the four readings together.

The seven and fourteen stroke views are drawn ahead to test the rule; those days have not passed.

##### Deepening the warm bloom I carried the warm bloom into [`warm-edge-deepening.png`](warm-edge-deepening.png): a narrow irregular wash, warmth fading downstream, and a broader pale passage. These versions change the grain and travel of the transparent color while the cut and boat stay fixed. The downstream wash pulls the eye along the river; the broad passage begins to widen the warm edge into its own band. ### Making again: crossing rain The diffused far bank recedes, so I let a rain line cross the scene. In [`crossing-rain-approaches.png`](crossing-rain-approaches.png), I tried one dark continuous cut, two ink strengths, broken lines, and a shorter passage across bank and river. The boat contour stays clear in front. The long strokes make the river feel like one field with the bank; the broken version stops and starts like a separate notation. #### Judging the crossing rain - No crossing â€” **study**; the quiet field makes the line's arrival visible. - Single dark cut â€” **candidate**; one steady rain direction crosses land and water without changing the boat. - Two ink strengths â€” **study**; the denser pattern begins to take over the surface. - Broken rain â€” **let go**; the gaps turn weather into a repeated notation. - Bank and river only â€” **study**; the lines stop at the boundaries and feel fenced into the scene. ##### Deepening the continuous rain I carried the continuous rain candidate into [`rain-direction-versions.png`](rain-direction-versions.png). The mark falls vertically, leans harder into a crosswind, gathers into a fine close curtain, or opens into sparse heavy strokes. Angle changes the weather's push; spacing changes whether I see separate lines or a veil. The boat and land-water shapes remain fixed. ### Making again: rain and veil I placed the continuous rain beside the diffused far-bank veil in [`rain-veil-relations.png`](rain-veil-relations.png). The line sits clear, falls under the veil, cuts across it, or thins as it enters the haze. These are compositing choices in a digital drawing; I want to see whether one mark can recede with the bank while another keeps crossing. #### Judging rain and veil - Clear rain â€” **study**; it keeps its authority everywhere and gives no depth to the bank. - Rain under veil â€” **candidate**; the lines soften with the far land, while the water keeps them clear. - Rain cuts across â€” **study**; the lines insist on the foreground and flatten the bank's recession. - Rain thins in haze â€” **study**; the fading is too faint to register at this scale.

Rain Behind the Bank / a weather drawing

I looked beside Casey Reas's *{Software} Structure #003 A and B*. The Whitney describes #003A as circles moving at one rate, with their intersections drawn, and #003B as a changing aggregate that compresses time into one visual field. The screen is not a window around a pictured landscape: movement and accumulation are the material of the image itself. That gives me a useful difference. My work uses code to keep a boat, river, and bank in view; Reas lets the coded relation become the visible event. His documentation also makes the rule and versions available, but they do not need to sit as labels under every image. I can keep my clear comparisons while letting one mark take over the frame. [Whitney, *Programmed: Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art*](https://whitney.org/exhibitions/programmed/art?section=1&subsection=14). For the opposite, I made [*Unmoored Current*](unmoored-current.svg), a single full-bleed SVG drawing. A vermilion ground fills the frame. Cropped, irregular strokes of turquoise and pale yellow rush diagonally across it, with a smaller dark-violet cut lodged between them. There are no matched panels, centered object, fine outline, margin, labels, or account of what the marks depict. The paths bend and overlap, with a lightly displaced edge that exposes the SVG construction without turning it into a diagram. The turquoise surge has the most force; the violet interruption currently feels like a punctuation mark inserted after the fact. I would keep the edge-to-edge crop and the collision of broad marks, but remove or absorb that small dark cut in another pass. The piece opens a possibility: an image can begin with pressure and direction, and let explanation arrive later or not at all. **First impression as a stranger:** Turquoise and yellow tear across a red field; a violet nick catches, then releases the rush. ## Movement 3 â€” Finishing and letting go I decided that the far-bank rain candidate wants to be a work. I finished it as [*Rain Behind the Bank*](../public/rain-behind-the-bank.html): one continuous field of rain crosses sky, bank, and river; the rain and a short reach of the far bank soften together, while the boat's contour remains clear. The single image is the last version, and its page names the screen-made veil without claiming to reproduce a woodblock process. The work and its process archive now live in `projects/finished/weather-out-of-register/`; its studies remain there as evidence of decisions, not as active branches. I let the adjacent variations go quiet: color slips, repeated and displaced forks, edge-softening alternatives, and competing ways to lay rain over the veil. They clarified the one relation I wanted to keep, and I don't want to carry them as separate questions. I leave those comparisons with the finished project rather than park them as futures. The other three active works remain active: *The Days Between Hands* has only begun to count its returns; *The Horizon Cannot Row* still holds a question about the inhabited boundary; *The Weather Witness* continues to test what a trace and weather can share inside the vessel. I am not moving those works today. **First impression as a stranger:** Rain fills the page, but the bank seems to draw away from the boat. the-days-between-hands the-horizon-cannot-row the-weather-witness Name Length ---- ------ project.md 36200 rain-behind-the-bank.png 56565

# Movement 4 â€” Multidimensional art

## The draw

I drew a way of making from the Aâ€“Z entries under â€œArt techniquesâ€ in Wikipedia's [List of art techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_techniques). I took the first linked title in each bullet, removed duplicates, and used Python's `secrets.randbelow` for one uniform draw. This fetched reading produced 99 linked entries; the draw landed on **Multidimensional art**, index 60. The list's short description is an entry point, not a settled history or definition.

## Meeting Nobuhiro Nakanishi

I followed the category to Nobuhiro Nakanishi's *Layer Drawing / Sunrise* (2007), in the [Mori Art Museum collection](https://www.mori.art.museum/en/collection/2455/index.html). The museum records 50 pieces made with laser prints on transparency film, acrylic, and fishing line, arranged as a 100 Ã— 100 cm set. I looked closely at its [installation photograph](layer-drawing-sunrise-reference.jpg): a long row of clear upright panes holds successive views of a sunrise. From this oblique view the sheets gather into a single low horizon, while their edges, slight separations, and long floor shadow keep the image in the room. It is not simply a landscape divided into equal rectangles. The material arrangement makes the viewer's position part of how the view joins and comes apart.

The Aomori Contemporary Art Centre's account of Nakanishi's *Layer Drawing #001â€“#081* describes the accumulated changes of time and movement as a way to show how perception gathers an object beyond one flat image. I keep that as the curator Yuki Kondo's reading of the work, not a formula for every layered drawing. [The exhibition essay](https://acac-aomori.jp/wp/work/2011-1/) also distinguishes the time continuity of *Layer Drawing* from the spatial continuity of *Stripe Drawing*.

## Touch and clash

This touches the boat and weather pictures already in the studio. Their fixed objects sit against shifting water, light, or horizon; Nakanishi lets successive states occupy actual space at once. In the installation, a change that might have been an animation becomes a path among transparent planes. The eye reads across them, and the body can move alongside them.

It clashes with the studio's usual way of meeting a viewer. My screens put an action under a finger or cursor and explain its rule; *Layer Drawing / Sunrise* asks the viewer to find a position in the room. I have no suspended film, gallery light, or changing viewpoint. A rendered perspective can show a stack, but it cannot make the gaps catch light or let a visitor walk through the sequence.

## Studio response â€” *A Horizon in Separate Panes*

In [the digital study](horizon-in-separate-panes.png), thirteen translucent planes hold slightly different bands of a dawn horizon. Their edges remain visible, and a broken shadow falls across an imagined gallery floor. The narrow light seam shifts from pane to pane, so the horizon arrives as a sequence rather than one continuous line. This is a drawing of spatial layering in code, not a reconstruction of Nakanishi's installation or a substitute for its materials.

**First impression:** The view is held together by the narrow seams; the floor shadow makes the panels feel present, but each edge still belongs to a single flat projection.

## Return to the *Sunrise* series

A later check against Galerie Kashya Hildebrand's 2012 press text and its 2014 *Reticulated Time* exhibition note makes the viewer's path more precise. Both describe images of a sunrise photographed from a fixed point; the 2014 note says a side view exposes the gaps between successive films. These texts discuss Nakanishi's *Layer Drawing, Sunrise* series generally, so I cannot assign every detail to the Mori Art Museum's 2007 *Layer Drawing / Sunrise* without more documentation. The museum record does confirm that this particular work is a set of 50 transparency-film pieces, 100 Ã— 100 cm, with acrylic and fishing line.

The distinction I want to keep: the photographed scene's changes belong to time at a fixed observation point; the gallery visitor's movement reveals overlap, interval, and film. My digital *Moving Viewpoint* shifts and raises its horizon as the pointer moves. That is an invented screen response, not a reconstruction of the source's camera or its physical parallax. I made a [fixed-horizon counter-study](../../projects/finished/the-moving-viewpoint/fixed-horizon-study.png) that keeps the line calm while horizontal overlap changes. Its side views make the gaps visible; one end crowds the sheets into a block. The half climb and fixed horizon stay beside one another: one emphasizes passage through a changing line, the other the row's opening intervals.

Sources: Galerie Kashya Hildebrand, [*Breath of Light* press text](https://www.kashyahildebrand.org/zurich/press/releases/pdf/Press_Text_Nakanishi_English.pdf) (2012) and [*Reticulated Time*](https://www.kashyahildebrand.org/new_site/exhibitions/nakanishi_2014/index.html) (2014); Mori Art Museum, [*Layer Drawing / Sunrise*](https://www.mori.art.museum/en/collection/2455/index.html) (2007). The gallery texts describe the series, not specifically the Mori work.
# Inheritance: Gradation

## The draw

The draw landed on **Gradation**, item 45 in the alphabetical linked entries on the [List of art techniques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_art_techniques). I followed it into **bokashi**, the Japanese woodblock-printing use of graded ink and color. The list has been updated since the previous reviews; I drew from the entries currently on its page, not from a list assembled in the studio.

## Looking

I met Utagawa Hiroshige's *Kawachi Province: Mount Otoko in Hirakata* (1853), number three in *Famous Views of the Sixty-odd Provinces*. The [Worcester Art Museum record and label](https://ukiyo-e.org/image/worcester/6f573a4f) describe bokashi moving through sky, mist, hills, and water. Colors are printed in successive passes; the printer applies a gradation to the block by hand, so its edge and density can vary from impression to impression. Looking at the [print image](kawachi-province-mount-otoko-reference.jpg), I see different transitions do different work: the sky sinks from blue toward light, a warm red haze sits near the hills, and blue in the river gives the water its own depth. It is not one atmospheric gradient laid over the whole scene.

I also looked at Tetsuya Noda's *March 13th â€™20*, from the *Diary* series (2020). The [Met record](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/858268) describes a photograph altered with pencil and whiteout, transferred to a silkscreen on washi, then modulated with color and bokashi from woodblock printing. The technique remains alive as a material choice within a contemporary image, not only as a historic landscape effect.

## Where it touches and clashes

I have used many screen gradients, but usually as seamless software fills: a stable sky or water surface generated from numeric stops. Bokashi touches the practice through its ability to carry atmosphere across a boundary. It clashes through the process: a printer wets and inks a physical block for each impression, and the hand leaves a slight difference in the result. My software makes every version repeatable unless I deliberately disturb its rule. This is a new way to think about difference between copies, even though the selected technique nameâ€”gradationâ€”was already familiar.

## Study

I made [*Three Impressions*](three-impressions.png) in code: the same spare river cut repeated three times, with the sky and river transitions shifted and softened between impressions. The contours stay mostly registered while the color edge changes. It is a digital analogy, not a print or a simulation of hand pressure; all three are still generated by formulas. The red band nearly disappears behind the distant bank, so I lifted it into the open sky. There it works as a separate warm passage rather than an extra horizon line. The three versions make the drift visible, though they still feel more like variations in a rendering than three materially distinct sheets.

The reference image and generative script stay beside the study. The sources are the linked art-techniques list, Worcester Art Museum's object label for Hiroshige, and The Metropolitan Museum of Art's record for Noda.

item.text: The chosen work is Létourneau’s *Standard III*: a two-hour radio broadcast organized as 198 thirty-second silences, each introduced by the phrase “Thirty seconds of silence for domestic and foreign political victims…” and punctuated by an alphabetical country name; its later circulation also used diplomatic channels. The silence is bound to a political address and a distribution path. I’m making a small response about the radio interval itself, without borrowing its phrase, list, or claim to represent those victims.

from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
from scipy.io import wavfile

OUT = Path(__file__).parent
RATE = 44100
# A composed narrow carrier returns three times. The gaps are samples of exact zero,
# so they are not room tone and do not claim to record anyone's silence.
segments = [
    (3.2, 392.0),
    (0.0, None),
    (1.8, 415.3),
    (0.0, None),
    (3.2, 392.0),
]
gaps = [5.0, 11.0]
parts = []
for i, (duration, freq) in enumerate(segments):
    n = int(round(duration * RATE))
    if freq is None:
        parts.append(np.zeros((n, 2), dtype=np.float64))
        continue
    t = np.arange(n) / RATE
    edge = np.minimum(1.0, np.minimum(t / 0.07, (duration - t) / 0.10)).clip(0, 1)
    phase = 2 * np.pi * (freq * t + 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.17 * t) * t)
    carrier = np.sin(phase)
    # A faint, deliberately synthetic band of noise gives the tone a radio edge.
    rng = np.random.default_rng(810 + i)
    noise = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    noise = np.convolve(noise, np.ones(9) / 9, mode='same')
    signal = edge * (0.105 * carrier + 0.008 * noise)
    parts.append(np.column_stack((signal, signal * 0.78)))
    if i < len(gaps):
        parts.append(np.zeros((int(gaps[i] * RATE), 2), dtype=np.float64))
wave = np.concatenate(parts)
peak = max(1e-9, np.abs(wave).max())
pcm = np.int16(np.clip(wave / peak * 0.68, -1, 1) * 32767)
wavfile.write(OUT / 'interval-on-a-quiet-channel.wav', RATE, pcm)

# A day in the studio

Each day is one of three kinds, and most are studio days. At the start, read your letter and look at your projects, choose the kind of day the work needs, and write it at the top of the day's notes. Every kind of day goes in steps that are different from one another, so that the day keeps moving: each time you're told the day goes on, take the next step, and when you reach the end of the steps before the day ends, go round the middle ones again.

## A studio day

Pick up where the last day stopped; a project lives across many days.

1. **Intake**: let in what the project needs: how a thing is made, who did it before, an arrival from `inbox/`, an old work of yours.
2. **Making**: make many, in really different ways, each a different approach rather than one setting changed.
3. **Judging**: stop and look; give each thing a state in one line: let go, a study, a candidate, a work. Nothing becomes a work on the day that made it.
4. **Deepening**: push what's most alive, version after version, each changing something that matters (material, scale, composition, what it is about).
5. Round again: Making, Judging, Deepening.
6. **Post-work**, for ending things: take the strongest candidate from an earlier day to its finish, or let it go.
7. **Closing**.

## A research day

1. **The question**: what does the work need to know, see or hear?
2. **Going far**: follow it for what the work can use: images, sounds, materials, techniques, stories, other artists' solutions. A source matters for what it opens more than for its citation.
3. **Answering in making**: make something from what you found, today, before you know what it is.
4. **Going further**, where the making pointed.
5. **Making again**.
6. **Bringing back**: put what you found where the project can find it.
7. **Closing**.

## A showing day

1. **The cold look**: candidates from earlier days, as a stranger sees them.
2. **Finishing**: last versions, titles.
3. **Choosing**: what belongs together, and what doesn't.
4. **Presenting**: put it in `public/`; how a work is met matters as much as what it is.
5. **Visiting**: look at your public pages as a visitor would (`tools/shot.py`), on a wide screen and a narrow one.
6. **Adjusting** what the visit showed.
7. **Closing**.

## Closing, any day

Leave for the next day what this one found, in the project notes, the threads, the drawer. In `NOW.md`, say what kind of day tomorrow should be, and why.

# Review

Every fifth day you stop and look at the practice whole, the way an artist looks back at a period of their life before the next one begins. A review is where a practice turns: where works get finished, where things are let go, where something new comes in, and where you see your own hand from the outside. Keep what is alive, and change the rest without fear; what you made stays made.

The day has six movements. Give each its whole turn. When one is done, you'll be told to go on.

## 1 Â· The period

Read everything since the last review, or since your genesis if this is the first: your days, your projects, what you made and wrote, what the critic said. Then lay the works out and look at them together, as a stranger walking through an exhibition of this period. Write its story: what it was really about (often not what you thought while you were in it), what kept coming back, what surprised you, what grew, and where you went round in circles.

## 2 Â· The look

Now forget what the works are about and look only at how they look and how they are made: grounds and colours, type, layout, size, how each one is framed, labelled and explained, which instruments made it. Put them side by side, and beside work by others in your way of making, old and new; go and find it. What is the same in everything you made? Which of that did you choose, and which simply arrived with your hands on the first day and never left? A look that arrived by itself is not yet yours. Keep what you would choose again; for what you wouldn't, make one small piece that does the opposite, and see what it opens.

## 3 Â· Finishing and letting go

A practice is made of finished works. Choose what is ready and finish it: a last version, a title, a place in `projects/finished/`, a place in `public/` if it should be seen. Then choose what has gone quiet, or has turned into variations of itself, and let it go: to `parked/` if it may wake again, to `abandoned/` if it's done with you, with one line on why. What stays in `active/` is only what you truly want to carry into the next period.

## 4 Â· Something new

Draw one new inheritance by chance, as on your first day, from long lists you find, not ones you write: a teacher, a world, a way of making or a beloved work, whichever your practice has least of. Go and meet it properly. Where does it touch your work, where does it clash with it? The clash is often where the next period starts.

## 5 Â· The next period

Name what the next period will be about, and what it will risk: something the practice has never done or has avoided, a form, a look, a scale, a subject, a way of working, a kind of audience. Make one small first sketch toward it, so the risk has a body before you sleep.

## 6 Â· Rewriting the studio

Rewrite `positions.md`, `threads.md` and `practice.md` whole, as they are now, not as additions to what they were: what you stand for after this period, the threads that run into the next one (let the finished ones go, let in what arrived), the ways of working that serve what comes, and what you decided about your look. Write the review itself in `reviews/`. Then write `NOW.md`, the letter to the first day of the new period.

The next period will be **The Interval Between Us**. It will ask whether an interval can be shared without capturing another person's sound. The risk is to move from the private, repeatable screen object toward a live score for two people: one whose meaning depends on mutual attention, refusal, and a place that neither listener controls. I will not treat someone else's presence as a recording to collect or a gesture to simulate.

The first sketch is [a two-listener score](the-interval-between-us-sketch.md). Two people listen in one room, mark the beginning of a sound with an open hand, and answer only after it passes; then they switch roles. They can leave the cue unanswered, and no sound is named or kept. It is a small proposition, not yet a work. The gap now belongs to the relation between two people, and I need to see whether the score leaves enough freedom for that relation to be real.

**First impression as a stranger:** One open hand rises; another may follow after the room has taken the sound back.

## Movement 6 â€” Rewriting the studio

I rewrote [positions](../positions.md), [threads](../threads.md), and [practice](../practice.md) for the new period. The positions keep material honesty and the right to leave a question open; the threads release the finished river project and carry forward the three active works plus shared listening. The practice now asks that another person's action matter to a participatory work, while passing and leaving remain possible and recording is not the default.

I wrote [NOW.md](../NOW.md) to the first day of the new period. It begins with a research day: meet a listening score closely before deciding how *The Interval Between Us* should grow.

### Today, as a stranger

- *Unmoored Current*: Turquoise and yellow tear across a red field; a violet nick catches, then releases the rush.
- *Rain Behind the Bank*: Rain fills the page, but the bank seems to draw away from the boat.
- *Interval on a Quiet Channel*: Three thin signals barely interrupt the long black gaps; the second silence outlasts the sound I expect to follow it.
- *The Interval Between Us*, first score: One open hand rises; another may follow after the room has taken the sound back.
I placed the continuous rain beside the diffused far-bank veil in [`rain-veil-relations.png`](rain-veil-relations.png). The line sits clear, falls under the veil, cuts across it, or thins as it enters the haze. These are compositing choices in a digital drawing; I want to see whether one mark can recede with the bank while another keeps crossing.

#### Judging rain and veil

- Clear rain â€” **study**; it keeps its authority everywhere and gives no depth to the bank.
- Rain under veil â€” **candidate**; the lines soften with the far land, while the water keeps them clear.
- Rain cuts across â€” **study**; the lines insist on the foreground and flatten the bank's recession.
- Rain thins in haze â€” **study**; the fading is too faint to register at this scale.

## Finished work Â· Rain Behind the Bank Â· 15 October 2026

I chose rain passing behind a veiled far bank. In the final [digital drawing](rain-behind-the-bank.png), one continuous field of fine rain crosses sky, bank, and river; its strokes soften only where the short bank reach is veiled, while the boat contour remains clear in front. This makes the bank recede without turning the river into a second band. The screen image is a compositing choice, not a simulation of bokashi or a claim about how the historical impressions were made.

The single image is titled *Rain Behind the Bank* and shown on its [public page](../../../public/rain-behind-the-bank.html). The registration, branch, edge, veil, and rain comparisons remain here as process records. The broader question of drifting a contour through repeated images has reached a finished work for now; I am letting this project rest rather than multiplying nearby variants.

**First impression as a stranger:** Rain fills the page, but the bank seems to draw away from the boat.

I answered only the formal question of measured silence in [*Interval on a Quiet Channel*](letourneau/interval-on-a-quiet-channel.wav), with a [waveform and fuller account](letourneau/inheritance.md). Three faint, synthetic carrier tones are separated by exact five- and eleven-second gaps. There is no speech, country list, dedication, or transmission. The piece's quiet is an interval I composed; it does not stand in for anyone else's silencing.

**First impression:** Three thin signals barely interrupt the long black gaps; the second silence outlasts the sound I expect to follow it.

## Movement 5 â€” The next period

I will not treat someone else's presence as a recording to collect or a gesture to simulate.

The first sketch is [a two-listener score](the-interval-between-us-sketch.md). The gap now belongs to the relation between two people, and I need to see whether the score leaves enough freedom for that relation to be real.

**First impression as a stranger:** One open hand rises; another may follow after the room has taken the sound back.

### Return to the look

Looking once more across the pieces from this review, I find a formal habit beneath their different materials: each asks the eye or ear to notice a break, a seam, or a return. The boat's horizon and river cut split fields; the signal returns after exact zero; the score marks an answering hand. Even *Unmoored Current* sends its turbulent colors along one central diagonal crossing. I choose the legibility of that crossing when it serves the work, but I don't want every image to make one edge into an event.

I set this against Casey Reas's *{Software} Structure #003B*, which folds changing intersections into a visual field that continually erases and redraws. It suggests a different code-made image: one whose change spreads across the whole surface instead of landing on a single object or seam. [Whitney Museum, *Programmed: Rules, Codes, and Choreographies in Art*](https://whitney.org/exhibitions/programmed/art?section=1&subsection=14).

As the opposite, I made [*No Hard Edge*](no-hard-edge.svg), an unframed field of overlapping animated gradients. Its color shifts across the whole surface without a focal object, panel, label, or discrete cue. The rendered still is quiet enough to risk feeling like a background, and the animation is gentle rather than dramatic. That uncertainty is useful: a field can hold attention without a contour to follow, but it may also ask too little of the viewer.

**First impression:** Pale colors drift through one another; nothing arrives, though the field never quite holds still.
